Case/data description

Climate Migration Tweet Dataset (Synthetic Version)

Acknowledgement: Thank you dra. Sercan Kiyak for generating the Tweet dataset and description of the data

  • Overview

This dataset is derived from an original Twitter collection focused on public discussions of climate migration (refugees displaced etc). The source data contained tweets referring to climate-induced displacement, refugees, and related political debates. From the original multilingual dataset, only three language groups were retained: • German (de) • Spanish (es) • Dutch (nl) These languages were chosen because they represented the largest clusters of activity in the corpus.

  • Time Period

Tweets were filtered to the period between 15 November 2019 and 31 December 2019, during which the volume of conversation was highest. This timeframe includes two key climate-related events: • The COP25 conference (2-13 December 2019, originally planned in Chile, later held in Madrid) • The European Parliament’s declaration of a climate emergency (28 November 2019)

  • Ethical Anonymization and Transformation

To make the data suitable for teaching and training, several steps were taken to fully anonymize and transform the texts:

  1. Metadata removal: All identifiable user information such as usernames, mentions, and links were replaced with placeholders (. For example: Original tweet: “@Merkel @Junger wir in Europa Klimanotstand haben sind wir ja auch Klimaflüchtlinge. Wo können wir hin?” (fake tweet) Anonymized tweets: “[user] [link] wir in Europa Klimanotstand haben sind wir ja auch Klimaflüchtlinge. Wo können wir hin?”

  2. Metadata retention: Only the following non-sensitive metadata were retained:

  • date (tweet date)
  • language (original tweet language)
  1. Translation and paraphrasing: Tweets were translated into English and paraphrased to preserve meaning and tone while preventing traceability to the original text. This used Llama3 for both tasks This process ensured that none of the resulting texts could be reverse-engineered to identify individual users.
  • Synthetic Tweet Generation

To expand the dataset (we had about 1800 non-ReTweet tweets, to make them about 5000 in order to make the model training more reliable), synthetic tweets were generated (instead of collecting new tweets). Two locally run small language models (lightweight versions of AI text generators like GPT) were used to create artificial tweets that looked similar to real ones: * Llama 3 (a small number of these were similar to paraphrased ones so deduplicated) * Gemma 3 Each paraphrased tweet served as input to these models, which generated new, semantically related tweets inspired by the same topic and sentiment. The outputs were NOT reviewed fully. Moreover see the final section about the evaluation.

  • Final Dataset

  • Original tweets (after filtering): n = 1862

  • Paraphrased and synthetic tweets combined: ≈ n = 5000

  • Columns retained: id (1 to X numbers) date language (the original text language) text (anonymised/synthetic text)

The dataset thus contains both transformed (paraphrased) and model-generated (synthetic) examples mixed. No original text, usernames, or links are included.

  • Limitations: Tone & Model Bias in Paraphrases/Synthetic Text

While the dataset aims to preserve the subject and stance of the original tweets, we observe a systematic tone shift introduced by the paraphrasing and synthetic generation steps. In particular: * Paraphrases and synthetic tweets skew more supportive of climate-migration and climate policy than the original discourse—especially in German (de), likely also in Dutch, where many tweets are in reality skeptical, ironic, or sarcastic. * This shift likely reflects alignment biases of the language models (LLMs), which tend to produce pro-refugee / pro-green framings and to smooth out sarcasm, irony, and antagonistic stances. * As a result, the transformed texts do not faithfully represent the full polarity present in the original timelines. They are best treated as didactic approximations for methods training—not as a ground-truth sample of public sentiment!

When viewing hashtags by country, it quickly becomes apparent that the three countries share the five most frequently used hashtags, but in a different order and with different distributions. For example, #climateRefugees is the most frequently used hashtag in all countries. Preprocessing

clean_tweet_text <- function(text) {
  
  # Convert to lowercase
  text <- str_to_lower(text)
  
  # Remove [user] and [link]
  text <- str_remove_all(text, "\\[user\\]|\\[link\\]")
  
  # Remove URLs (http or https)
  text <- str_remove_all(text, "http\\S+|https\\S+")
  
  # Remove @mentions
  text <- str_remove_all(text, "@\\w+")
  
  # Remove hastags
  text <- str_remove_all(text, "#\\w+")

  #Remove single letter
  text <- str_remove_all(text, "\\b[a-z]\\b")
  
  # Remove everything that is not a letter (a-z), a space (\\s), 
  # We replace them with a space to prevent words from sticking together.
  text <- str_replace_all(text, "[^a-z0-9\\s#']", " ")
  
  # Remove any extra spaces
  text <- str_squish(text)
  
  return(text)
}


cl_tweets <- tweets %>% mutate(cleaned_tweets = clean_tweet_text(text))

lema_tweets <- cl_tweets %>% unnest_tokens(words, cleaned_tweets) %>% filter(!words %in% c("let","isn","s","climate",stopwords("en"))) %>% mutate(lem = lemmatize_words(words)) %>% group_by(id) %>% summarise(lema_text = paste(lem, collapse = ' ')) 

tweets_df <- merge(x = cl_tweets, y = lema_tweets, by ="id", all.x = T)

A. We started by tokenising our tweets. This makes it easier to clean up, filter out stop words, and lemmatise each word.

B. Next, we cleaned the tokens. Below is an explanation of each cleaning step we used:

  • Lower all the tokens: We did this in order to better seize all the different variants of the stopwords we wish to remove from the corpus.

  • We remove all the [link] and [user]: These are placeholders that do not provide us with any semantic information that is important for the current analysis, as they are repetitive in all tweets.

  • We additionally removed all the links and mentions (again): Although we have no doubt that the corpus provider has already done so, we felt it might be important to remove the links and mentions again in case some had not been properly filtered. We could have skipped this step, but as a precaution, we decided to do it anyway.

  • We removed the hashtags: this was after considerable discussion about whether they should be retained. In this dataset, nearly all tweets contain the same hashtags, effectively turning them into stopwords due to their high frequency and limited semantic value. Because our analysis includes exploring collocations, retaining these hashtags would bias the results, as they tend to co-occur and would dominate the collocation patterns. In addition, since we intend to apply the same preprocessing pipeline to the topic modelling step, keeping the hashtags could negatively affect topic detection, given that the same tags appear in almost every tweet.

  • We removed isolated letter: Initially, we did not remove isolated letters, but after pre-processing, we found that certain isolated letters with no semantic meaning were captured at a high frequency. We therefore decided to remove single-letter tokens from our corpus.

  • We removed everything that is not a letter (a-z) or a space (\s) and replaced them with a space to prevent words from sticking together. This mainly removes punctuation marks and emojis. For collocations and topic modelling, punctuation marks and emojis are irrelevant, as the algorithm used for this task (according to our research) does not capture their semantic value. However, it is important to note that another pre-processing pipeline is required for sentiment analysis, as some algorithms, such as Vader, capture the semantic values of punctuation marks and emojis.

  • Finally we removed extra spaces. extra spaces are noises which have not semantic values.

C. We lemmatized the cleaned tokens to reduce each word to its root form. This step was deemed necessary because it consolidates different inflected or derived variants of a word, thereby reducing the sparsity of the document–term matrix (DTM). Lemmatization also improves our ability to capture meaningful collocations and enhances the quality of subsequent topic modelling.

D. Finally, we gathered the cleaned and lemmatised tokens in a column named lema_text, which is the text field we will use to create our corpus.

The collocation shows that the words ‘spin-dry’ and “corridor” tend to appear together. After a little research, we discovered that the ‘dry corridor’ is a dry tropical forest that is affected by climate change. But we didn’t understand where the prefix ‘spin’ came from. So we decided to delve deeper into our research on lemmatised tweets containing the word ‘spin-dry’.

tweets_df[1773, ]$text
## [1] "\"Food insecurity grips Guatemala's Dry Corridor, with millions projected to be climate-displaced in Central America by 2050 🌊 #ClimateMigration #DisasterRelief\""
tweets_df[1773, ]$cleaned_tweets
## [1] "food insecurity grips guatemala' dry corridor with millions projected to be climate displaced in central america by 2050"
tweets_df[1773, ]$lema_text
## [1] "food insecurity grip guatemala spin-dry corridor million project displace central america 2050"

The original tweet correctly mentions ‘Dry corridor’, the cleaned tweet also correctly retains ‘dry corridor’, but the lemmatised version of the tweet adds the prefix “spin” to the adjective ‘dry’. This is surprising, as we would not expect such a change from the lemmatisation process. After some research, we discovered that the lemmatisation algorithm had confused the adjective ‘dry’ with the verb ‘dry’ (to dry clothes) and had therefore added the prefix “spin” to what it considered to be a verb in order to reduce the verb ‘dry’ to its root form.

This reminds us that we must always check the text after applying various pre-processing steps. In summary, the terms ‘dry’ and “corridor” are actually the most frequent collocation in our corpus, which makes more sense than ‘spin-dry corridor’.

The six other most frequent collocations are those that one would expect to find in a corpus dealing with climate migration.

  • Preprocessing:

For the “vader” package specifically, less preprocessing than usual is required. In the following chunk, we are removing placeholders/stray URLs, retweets markers, and replacing hashtags with words.

data_vader <- read_csv('/Users/PaulMUTAMBA/Documents/Old Pc/KUL QASS/Collecting and Analysing for SDS/Assignements/tweets_final.csv') %>%
  mutate(
    text = as.character(text),
    text = iconv(text, to = "UTF-8", sub = ""),
    text = str_replace_all(text, "\\[(USER|LINK)\\]", " "),
    text = str_replace_all(text, "\\bhttps?://\\S+", " "),
    text = str_replace_all(text, "^RT\\s+", " "),
    text = str_replace_all(text, "(^|\\s)#([\\p{L}\\p{N}_]+)", "\\1\\2"),
    text = str_squish(text)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(text), text != "") %>%
  distinct(id, text, .keep_all = TRUE)

Selection sentiment package

Considering the nature of our dataset (twitter corpus, climate migration topic) and goals (sentiment analysis), the following packages were considered:

  • just “tidytext” and its lexicons (not chosen):

This is one of the more simple and straightforward ways of conducting sentiment analyses as of now, given that this package does not offer any built-in ways of handling negations, punctuation nuances, emojis, caps, amplifiers, etc.

The good thing about this option is that there are different lexicons available (“nrc”, “afinn”, “bing”, “loughran”) — but we are excluding “nrc” as it is used in the following task and “loughran” since it claims to be developed for financial contexts specifically, — which leaves us with “afinn” and “bing”.

Technically, we could employ both of them in our context, since “afinn” dictionary was specifically developed for the twitter context, and “bing” is a roughly “all-purpose” lexicon (though it was initially created for customer reviews).

But nonetheless, it would still be interesting to try and take into account negations, punctuation, emojis, and other potential features. Thus, unless we want to build our own set of rules (which might be quite complicated and not necessarily worth the effort in terms of the resulting classification quality), we might as well prefer other options.

  • sentimentr (not chosen):

This is one of the more advanced packages that has the ability to comprehend negations, amplifiers, de-amplifiers, etc. natively. It also offers the flexibility to use different lexicons (including the ones mentioned above that generally fit our goals, the base lexicon is “bing” + “syuzhet” combined).

Punctuation, elongated words, caps usage are not treated automatically on the other hand. Unless we extend our dictionaries and create tokens for those features, they will not affect the analysis — which is already not by any means bad, but there are still more ideal packages that have those features built-in intrinsically.

  • sentiStrengthR (not chosen):

This is one of the two most advanced packages we could use for our analysis. sentiStrengthR employs negations, amplifiers, punctuation, repeated letters, emoji, etc. Its dictionary is specifically designed for short informal texts with continuous pos/neg strengths attributed to each token. sentiStrengthR was generally a viable option, however another package was preferred the for reasons stated below.

  • vader:

This is the second most advanced package, and also our package of choice. It handles ~nearly everything that sentiStrengthR handles, and a bit more (for instance, this package is supposed to be a bit more familiar with slang and complex grammatical constructions). Its dictionary contains more than 7500 tokens and is specifically tuned for the microblogs contexts. Vader also allows to add tokens to the vocabulary, as opposed to the sentiStrengthR.

How does it work?

Answer:

“Vader” package a dictionary(or rule)-based approach to sentiment analysis.

It has a built-in manually labelled dictionary with more than 7500 tokens, suitable for microblog context. Addition of other tokens is possible, but the documentation authors advise to have 10 people label any given new token independently, and only add tokens whose standard deviation doesn’t exceed 2.5

VADER follows the following steps in the implementation

  1. Sums all the valence scores of each word in the lexicon;

  2. Adjusts it according to the inner rules set (including the handling of punctuation, caps, emojis, degree modifiers, negations, slang/abbreviations, contrastive conjunctions);

  3. Normalizes the score to be between -1 and 1.

Typical thresholds for classification mentioned in the documentation.

if score >= 0,05 -> positive; if score <= -0,05 -> negative; else: neutral.

Sources: — https://vadersentiment.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html

Why is it not a good idea to use the sentiment dictionary of the books website?

Answer:

This dictionary has a binary division on positive and negative words, is pretty general, and also not really big in volume (around ~3600 words for negative and ~2000 for positive categories, respectively). It is not a good idea to use it for a number of reasons.

Firstly, this particular dictionary doesn’t fit our context of the climate migration tweets dataset precisely enough — we could benefit from something a little more intricate. In the grand scheme of things, we would want our dictionary/set of rules to be specifically tuned for our usage context to get the best possible accuracy out of our dictionary approach. There’s no reason to expect this dictionary to perform better than the ones specifically tuned for the microblogs context, or the ones bigger in size.

Another question that could be raised is the methodology of this dictionary. How many people had to agree on the positive/negative words’ labels for it to be finalized? We couldn’t find any information regarding this, so naturally it is also a point of concern — if it was labelled in its entirety by only one person, the bias might be too serious.

Sentiment analysis:

Let’s now apply vader to our preprocessed data.

Even though vader performs tokenization on its own, we are additionally tokenizing entire tweets by sentences to ensure that each sentence has equal weight in the final calculation of a given tweet’s sentiment.

Otherwise, an overwhelmingly positive or negative sentence may throw off the score of a tweet as a whole. But this step is more of a researcher’s preference — we decided to do it, and others might decide against it.

Our thresholds for the initial run are the ones recommended in vader documentation.

# Let's build a function that tokenizes tweets by sentences and calculates average compound score for each sentence in one tweet

vader_compound_mean <- function(x) {
  sents <- tokenize_sentences(x, strip_punct = FALSE, simplify = TRUE)
  if (length(sents) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  sc <- sapply(sents, function(s) as.numeric(get_vader(s)["compound"]))
  mean(sc, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Running vader itself
data_vader <- data_vader %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(vader_compound = vader_compound_mean(text)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # Let's try package recommended thresholds
    vader_label = case_when(vader_compound >= 0.05 ~ "positive", vader_compound <= -0.05 ~ "negative", TRUE ~ "neutral"))
  

data_vader %>% count(vader_label)
## # A tibble: 3 × 2
##   vader_label     n
##   <chr>       <int>
## 1 negative     2886
## 2 neutral       940
## 3 positive     1656

Interpretation: vader concluded that there are 2886 negative, 1656 positive, and 940 neutral tweets. Neutral category looks suspiciously small so let’s perform a quick validation.

Validation:

335 tweets were sampled from the entire dataset and then human-labelled as either negative, neutral, or positive (it’s a rather primitive check, we were only aiming at 10% CI).

# A little clean-up function because we found weird excel artefacts in some cells in our validation file
canon_label <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  x <- str_replace_all(x, "\u00A0", " ")
  x <- str_squish(tolower(x))
  x <- recode(x, "pos" = "positive", "neg" = "negative", "neu" = "neutral", .default = x)
  factor(x, levels = c("negative","neutral","positive"))
}

# Validation_vader is the inital dataset but with 335 added human labels
val <- read_excel("validation_vader.xlsx") %>%
  slice(1:335) %>%
  filter(!is.na(human_label)) %>%
  mutate(human_label = canon_label(human_label), vader_label_excel = canon_label(vader_label_pred))

# Confusion matrix
cm <- conf_mat(val, truth = human_label, estimate = vader_label_excel)
kable(cm$table, caption = "Confusion matrix (rows = observed, cols = predicted)")
Confusion matrix (rows = observed, cols = predicted)
negative neutral positive
negative 125 48 20
neutral 9 30 11
positive 11 33 48 
# Accuracy, Cohen's k, precision, recall, f1 (using macro estimators as each label is equally important to us)
overall_metrics <- bind_rows(
  accuracy(val, truth = human_label, estimate = vader_label_excel),
  kap(val, truth = human_label, estimate = vader_label_excel),
  precision(val, truth = human_label, estimate = vader_label_excel, estimator = "macro"),
  recall(val,    truth = human_label, estimate = vader_label_excel, estimator = "macro"),
  f_meas(val,    truth = human_label, estimate = vader_label_excel, estimator = "macro"))
overall_metrics 
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   .metric   .estimator .estimate
##   <chr>     <chr>          <dbl>
## 1 accuracy  multiclass     0.606
## 2 kap       multiclass     0.381
## 3 precision macro          0.590
## 4 recall    macro          0.580
## 5 f_meas    macro          0.558

Interpretation:

The overall accuracy is around 0.6, which is not bad. Precision is around 0.59 — around 59% of tweets’ classes are predicted correctly (on average); recall is around 0.58 — around 58% of true items in a class are recovered.

F-statistic is around 0.56 — not too bad as well (however we can see a drop from the other statistics, which means that we have problematic labels — “neutral” and “positive” have weaker quality of prediction, and it reflects in the CM as well). Cohen’s k is around 0.38, thus implies that vader still works better than random assignment of labels based on their relative “appearance chance” proportion.

In sum, our concerns about “neutral” category were justified (it is indeed problematic), however the labels themselves are not awful and still usable so we can proceed to the next task and interpret our outputs comfortably.

Evolution over time

Important climate-related events from the dataset description:

  • COP25 conference (2-13 December 2019);

  • European Parliament’s declaration of a climate emergency (28 November 2019).

Let’s take a look the evolution of predicted sentiments over time.

We will start with daily mean vader sentiments (overall scores):

# Choosing time range
data_vader <- data_vader %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2019-11-15"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-31"), !is.na(vader_compound))


# Calculating means with 95% CI ribbon for the daily mean (normal approximation)
daily <- data_vader %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
    mean_compound = mean(vader_compound, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(vader_compound, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = sd / sqrt(n), 
    ci95 = 1.96 * se, .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(roll7 = rollapply(mean_compound, width = 7, align = "right", fill = NA, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE))

# Our key events
events <- tibble(date  = as.Date(c("2019-11-28","2019-12-02","2019-12-13")))

# Making a visualisation of compound scores
p_daily <- ggplot(daily, aes(x = date, y = mean_compound)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_compound - ci95, ymax = mean_compound + ci95), alpha = .15) +
  geom_line(color = "cornflowerblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(color = "firebrick", method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "longdash") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(data = events, aes(xintercept = date), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(title = "Daily mean of vader sentiment (compound score)", subtitle = "15 Nov – 31 Dec 2019 (ribbon — 95% CI of daily mean; dashed lines are key events)", x = NULL, y = "Mean VADER (compound)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_daily
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Interpretation:

As we can see, in the period from 15/11/2019 to 31/12/2019, the daily mean scores are, for the most part, below 0.0 (most often sitting at [−0.10; −0.15]). It implies that the sentiment during this time period was, for the most part, mildly negative.

At the 28th of November (EP’s declaration of a climate emergency), we can see one of the lowest dips of a mean sentiment, and up until around 13th of December (near to the end of COP25) the sentiment remained overwhelmingly negative, and had even lower dips thorough.

After that, we can see that mean sentiment was getting not as negative. With many ribbons touching 0.0, we can even say that it got somewhat close to being neutral.

Even though the proportion of positive tweets increased in the late December, the mean is still close to zero because negative tweets are intensely negative, and positive tweets are generally only modestly positive.

Let’s also look at the daily proportions of labels:

# Making a visualisation of labels

byday_label <- data_vader %>% 
  count(date, vader_label, name = "n") %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

p_prop <- ggplot(byday_label, aes(x = date, y = prop, fill = vader_label)) +
  geom_area(alpha = .9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(title = "Daily proportion of vader labels", x = NULL, y = "Share of tweets") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = "Vader label"))

p_prop

Tells pretty much the same story as the previous plot. Negative sentiments have the highest share most od the days, with peaks in late November/early December. Positive sentiments climb back after around 13th of December. Actual “neutral” label is always the thinnest and, as we figured in the validation step, is problematic.

Topic modeling

How Many Topics?

As mentioned earlier, the same pre-processing pipeline used for the collocation stage is applied for theme modelling. We felt that removing hashtags and punctuation marks from the corpus helped to reduce noise that could affect the theme modelling process. Therefore lemmatised text was used as the text field for the corpus used for the topic modelling.

LDA requires specifying k, the number of topics, as a hyperparameter. To identify an appropriate value of k, we estimated multiple LDA models with different numbers of topics, ranging from two to twelve in increments of two. For each model, we extracted coherence, perplexity, and exclusivity scores to evaluate which number of topics provided the best overall trade-off across these metrics. Additionally, we repeated this entire procedure three times using different random seeds to assess whether the trade-offs were stable or driven by seed-specific variation.

tweet_corpus = corpus(tweets_df, docid_field = "id",
                         text_field = "lema_text") %>% 
  quanteda::tokens(remove_punct=T) %>%
  tokens_tolower %>% 
  dfm() %>% 
  dfm_trim(min_docfreq = 5, docfreq_type = "count")

library(topicdoc)
library(topicmodels)

results1 = list()
dtm = convert(tweet_corpus, to="topicmodels")

# We define our parameters
seeds_to_test <- c(123, 91, 42) # Three seeds randomly chosen
k_values <- c(2, 4, 8, 10, 12)    # The K-values

results_list <- list()

#For each seed we ran the LDA with different K topics
for (s in seeds_to_test) {
  for (k in k_values) {
    
    alpha <- 1 / ((1:k) + sqrt(k))
    
    lda <- LDA(dtm, k = k, control = list(seed = s, alpha = alpha))
    
    results_list[[paste(s, k, sep = "_")]] <- data.frame(
      seed = s,
      k = k,
      perplexity = perplexity(lda),
      coherence = mean(topic_coherence(lda, dtm)),
      exclusivity = topic_exclusivity(lda)
    )
  }
}

# We Combine all results into one big data frame
all_results_df <- bind_rows(results_list)
# We Pivot the data into a long format for ggplot
results_long <- all_results_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(perplexity, coherence, exclusivity),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  )


ggplot(results_long, aes(x = k, y = value, color = as.factor(seed), group = as.factor(seed))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("Number of topics (k)") +
  ylab("Metric Value") +
  labs(color = "Seed") +
  facet_grid(metric ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal()

Our goal is to achieve a high consistency and exclusivity score, along with a minimal perplexity score. The graph of the three metrics shows that k = 4 offers the best compromise with a seed number of 123.

With a seed of 91, the best compromise between the three metrics is again k = 4.

With a seed of 42, the best compromise between the three metrics is again k = 4. It appears that our corpus of tweets on climate immigration presents four main discussion themes. The next steps involve exploring and interpreting these four themes, and analyzing their relevance and significance to the corpus.

Running LDA

lda <- dtm %>% LDA(k=4, control = list(seed=123, alpha=1/1:10))

df_terms <- tidy(lda, "beta") ## beta score


df_top <- df_terms |>
  group_by(topic) %>% 
  slice_max(n = 10, beta) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  arrange(topic, beta) %>% 
  mutate(order = row_number())

df_top %>% 
  mutate(term = reorder_within(term, beta, topic)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(beta, term, fill = factor(topic))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
facet_wrap(~topic, scales = "free") +
scale_y_reordered() +
labs(
title = "Top Terms per Topic in Climate Migration Tweets",
x = "Word Importance (beta)",
y = NULL) +
theme_minimal()

Topic Interpretation

Based on the LDA analysis with k=4 topics, we can distinguish four distinct thematic clusters in the climate migration Twitter discourse: 1. Call to action and urgency: . The dominant terms: “change,” “need,” “action,” “urgent,” “crisis,” “impact,” “community,” “displacement,” “displace,” and “protect” suggest advocacy and emphasizes the severity of climate-induced displacement and the necessity for immediate intervention and action.

  1. German policy and integration: dominant terms like “refugee,” “germany,” “displace,” “individual,” “environmental,” “citizenship,” “german,” “migrant,” “asylum,” and “green” indicate discussions about how Germany handles environmental refugees. Also by skimming through tweets we can see that many of those discuss legal frameworks, and integration policies.

  2. Migration issue definition and solutions: With terms like “refugee,” “migration,” “issue,” “solution,” “just,” “environmental,” “focus,” “change,” and “address,” this cluster appears to focus on refugee issues as a result from climate change. Not only that, but upon reviewing the tweets we also see people who have problems with the way climate change issue and refugee issues are framed and some are okay with that and call for solutions.

  3. Humanitarian Impact and Scale: This topic emphasizes the magnitude and humanitarian dimensions of climate displacement. Terms such as “rise,” “force,” “crisis,” “home,” “displacement,” “due,” “million,” “sea,” “people,” and “flee” paint a picture of large-scale forced migration driven by environmental factors. Upon examining the top tweets we see a strong emphasis on rising sea levels, rising temperatures, and discplacement.

  rename_all(~paste0("Topic_", .))

  1. Formulate a clear conclusion.

Answer: The LDA results reveals that Twitter discourse on climate migration is multidimensional and has distinct and intersecting topics. The conversation spans from urgent calls for action (Topic 1) to specific policy contexts (Topic 2), from problem-solution framing (Topic 3) to humanitarian crisis scale(Topic 4).The corpus reflects climate migration as simultaneously an environmental crisis, a humanitarian emergency, a policy challenge, and a social justice issue.

  1. In your opinion, is LDA suited for this kind of corpus research question? What are its limitations in this specific research setup? Can you propose some follow-up research steps to take?

Answer: LDA is moderately well-suited for this corpus, but with important considerations: 1. Context: LDA treats words as independent and ignores context. 2.Sentiment: As we saw in topic 3, upon investigating the tweets, we saw that they used similar wordings but they meant opposite things. LDA does not allow the capturing of positive or negative sentiment. 3. Hashtag noise: as we noted earlier hashtags were a topic were we had whether or not to keep them and the degree to which they contribute to the answering of the research question. 4. Translantion of tweets : Due to the translation of the original text we may miss some pivotal semantic values. 5. Ai Generated tweets: the fact that the tweets are ai generated may have contributed to redundancy and skewing of the results.

But overall, LDA was an okay and quick method for exploring the data unsupervised.

Follow up steps for this research question could be:

1.Labelling the data and running sentiment analyses to see the sentiment per topic and capture the differnces between topics. This way it’ll help us see which topics produce more debates and critical conversations. 2. Temporal analysis: This way we can see how topics change over time and we can tie them to real world events which might give valuable insight. Additionally, we can collect new data from events that initiated large scale online discussions about climate migration. ex. COP26, etc.. 3. Analysis per country: since we have topic that was strongly tied to germany, it might be valuable to run analysis per country to see patterns within borders.

All analytical decisions—including interpreting keywords, determining topic meanings, and reviewing the tweets themselves—were made by us The AI was used only to help improve clarity and structure in our writing.

All AI responses were read and assesed for clarity and accuracy and edited accordingly. No analytical steps (data cleaning, modeling, coding, or topic generation) were performed by the AI. In many instances AI gave incoherent and wrong suggestions that we had to correct ourselves.
